body.text: How a 'healthy' schoolies week ended with a 15yo on life support
In the heart of a bustling Surfers Paradise, a 15-year-old boy lies almost motionless.
Blood pools around his head, faint breaths the only visible sign he is still alive.
A female police officer kneels by his side as a pack of teens runs into the night.
The video captured by CCTV and released by the court during hearings this week for 12 teens charged over the assault, provided a confronting contrast to the images of schoolies just 24 hours earlier.
A day prior, police had praised this year's cohort for their behaviour at the annual end of school celebrations on Queensland's Gold Coast.
"I walked the beat as a senior sergeant here 10 years ago, and you could guarantee at 2 o' clock near McDonalds, it was fight time," Superintendent Peter Miles told media on Monday.
"We're not getting any of that now."
In an instant, it all came crashing down, when an alleged act of "gratuitous violence" left a boy, a son, an aspiring barber, fighting for life.
Incident captured on CCTV
At 3am on Tuesday, a group of at least 12 teenagers allegedly bashed the 15-year-old Ipswich boy just metres from the official schoolies celebration area.
The attack left the victim with a broken jaw, at least 10 fractures, including one that extends to the base of his skull, and bleeding on the brain.
He has been on life support at Gold Coast University Hospital since, with scans on Thursday showing no signs of brain activity.
The boy's family has requested he not be named.
It is still unclear what sparked the incident, but the court has heard a network of cameras in Cavill Avenue captured the incident in horrifying detail.
Video released by the court shows the boy standing among a crowd near the Gold Coast's iconic Surfers Paradise sign when a group of teens approaches and the violence begins.
The boy escapes, sprinting down Cavill Avenue before his alleged attackers catch up and trip him to the ground.
As he curls into the foetal position, shielding his face, the teens kick and stomp his head and body, continuing even when he falls limp.
The footage shows crowds of revellers watching in shock, some filming the incident on their phones.
As police flood into view of the cameras, the teens scatter.
'Pack mentality'
Twelve Brisbane teenagers — all aged between 17 and 19 — have each been charged with acts intended to cause grievous bodily harm over the alleged attack.
At least four of them were registered schoolies.
In courtrooms where the charges have been heard, the attack has been described as "vicious", "prolonged", "callous", and showing "zero human empathy".
Police prosecutor Matt Gilles told a hearing for one of the adults charged that the "extreme gratuitous violence" could be described with two words: "pack mentality".
He told the court police would allege that at least some element of what happened on Tuesday morning was planned.
"There is evidence to suggest that there was a level of organisation to attend [Surfers Paradise] and assault the victim," Mr Gilles said.
'Lives irrevocably changed'
The incident came days after schoolies organisers and volunteers praised an "amazing shift" in the event's culture.
"[Young people] are swapping out the night-time activities and the risk-taking behaviour in the early hours of the morning," Red Frogs' Chris George said last Friday.
Detective Inspector Greg Aubort, who is leading the investigation, said it was a "sickening, violent assault".
"It mars what has otherwise been a very healthy [schoolies] event," he said.
"What's disappointing is the group mentality … this is a warning to those that roll around in groups and gangs: your lives can be irrevocably changed in minutes."
In the immediate aftermath of the violence, school leavers told the ABC the attack had left them on edge.
"I'm less keen to go out later at night. Before 12 is fine, but just walking the streets … it's actually a bit scary," Toowoomba graduate Caleb Baker said.
"I'd stay away from this area."
Police investigation continues
The parents of the 15-year-old victim this week released a statement, saying the incident had been "incredibly distressing" for everyone close to the boy.
"This has been made more difficult by videos and commentary relating to the incident circulating on social media," the parents wrote.
They said they were "overwhelmed" by the kindness they had received from the community.
But they requested privacy as they focus on their son's recovery and said they would not provide any further updates on his condition.
The Queensland government, which organises the official schoolies event, was today due to hold a press conference wrapping up the week-long celebration, but that has since been cancelled.
As a devastated family holds on to hope their son will survive his injuries, the police investigation into his assault continues.
"There are more people that we are looking for," Deputy Commissioner Cheryl Scanlon said on Thursday.
"Schoolies has in recent years been a very safe event for young people and that's how we'd like it to stay.
